## Response to Weakness #3

> The data scales used for RST (80k) and Logic-Distill (40k) differ substantially, which makes it difficult to attribute performance differences purely to the proposed methodology. Although Section 4.4 includes a scaling-law analysis, the discussion remains qualitative and does not include experiments where both methods are trained on exactly the same number of samples, making it unclear how much of the reported gain comes from logicality rather than data quantity.

We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. In our pipeline, Logic-Distill is obtained by filtering the full 80k candidate set (i.e., the "Direct-Distill" dataset) using our logicality metrics, so its final size is necessarily smaller than 80k. To enable a fair comparison at the same data scale, we evaluate the public baseline MegaScience, the "DD" baseline, and the "RST" variant when trained on 20k, 40k, and 60k samples; among these, the 20k and 40k settings are directly comparable to Logic-Distill. For each target size, all subsets are sampled from the same 80k pool with an identical protocol, ensuring comparable data distributions across methods.

**Appendix B (Tables 9-11) quantitatively reports these results: at the same 20k and 40k data scales**, Logic-Distill consistently outperforms the baselines on both the public physics benchmarks and the PhysLogic metric across all backbone models. **This suggests that the performance gains mainly come from the logicality-based selection rather than from using more training data.**

## Response to Weakness #4 (part 1/2)

> The evaluation heavily relies on the authors’ own logicality metrics (logical fidelity, causal connection, and inferential progress), which are derived from the same annotated nexus structure used for training. This creates a strong overlap between the training signal and the evaluation criteria. Without human judgments or external benchmarks, it is difficult to confirm whether higher metric scores truly correspond to more logically sound reasoning, or simply reflect closer alignment to the annotated schema. Moreover, the relationship between these logicality metrics and task accuracy has not been empirically demonstrated, leaving it unclear whether improvements in logicality genuinely translate into better reasoning performance.

We thank the reviewer for raising this concern. As described at the beginning of Section 4, our computational experiments are organized into two stages. In the first stage (Section 4.3), we use our logicality metrics as the evaluation criteria, but this is only to verify that our constructed methods can indeed enhance the logicality of LLM reasoning. As shown in Table 6, our two proposed datasets, in particular **"RST", which does not perform sampling directly on the F/O/P scores**, yield substantial improvements. In the second stage (Section 4.4), we conduct comparative experiments on a variety of external benchmarks. As shown in Table 7, our two constructed methods consistently and significantly outperform all baseline methods across all benchmarks. This demonstrates that our approach is **not merely overfitting to our own logical metrics** but, while improving scientific logicality, also substantially boosts the final performance of LLMs on multiple public physics question-answering tasks.

## Response to Weakness #1

> Lack of justification for using a sentence encoder to embed logical steps. While sentence encoder performs well on encoding contexts and general semantics, it may fail to differ subtle logical differences and especially hallucinations. Since the sentence embedding similarity is the basis for all proposed logical metrics, the authors should first verify the feasibility of using a sentence encoder for encoding logical reasoning steps.

Thanks, we employ a sentence encoder in a standard way as a low-level representation tool, as is common in many NLP tasks [1-3]. In our setting, it is only used to map each semantically coherent reasoning step and each logical nexus into a shared vector space. Each encoded unit (sentence) is a single, semantically self-contained step (or nexus) describing a specific intermediate quantity or relation in the derivation, rather than a long multi-sentence paragraph, which reduces the burden on the encoder and focuses the similarity computation on local content. **The resulting embedding similarities are intended to capture low-level semantic relatedness between model steps and logical nexuses, rather than to serve as a direct logical validity criterion.**

As described in Section 2.1, on top of these similarities we construct three higher-level metrics, $\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{P}$, to evaluate logicality. Specifically, these metrics respectively focus on (i) the alignment between the semantics of model-generated steps and the logical nexuses, (ii) the relative magnitudes and distribution of similarities across different steps, and (iii) the degree of repetition within a single reasoning trajectory.

To further address your concern, as detailed in our **Response to Weakness #2** below, we have conducted human evaluation which supports the feasibility of our logicality metrics.

[1] Das, S., Deb, N., Cortesi, A., & Chaki, N. (2021). Sentence embedding models for similarity detection of software requirements. SN Computer Science.

[2] Reimers, N., & Gurevych, I. (2019, November). Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks. In Proceedings of the 2019 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing and the 9th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing.

[3] https://sbert.net/examples/sentence_transformer/training/sts/README.html

## Response to Weakness #2

> Lack of analysis on the properties of the three logical metrics. These metrics are intuitively defined but not verified whether they truly reflect respective logical properties. I understand that verifying this is hard for the general case, but a few typical examples would also help.

Thank you for raising this point. **In the revised paper, we have added a case study section (Appendix J)**, which intuitively illustrates the overall patterns of examples with high and low scores along the three logical dimensions. The newly added parts are highlighted in red.

In addition, to more rigorously verify that the three logicality metrics we propose truly reflect the corresponding logical properties, we have added an empirical study on human–metric consistency. Specifically, we randomly sample 200 data instances from the constructed dataset. A human physics expert and ChatGPT-5 are each asked to assign a 1-10 logicality score to the reasoning process. We then compute the pairwise correlation coefficients and significance values between our averaged logicality scores (F/O/P), the human ratings, and the LLM ratings. The experimental results are presented in Table R2-1. **These results demonstrate that higher scores assigned by our metrics consistently correspond to more logically sound reasoning, as evidenced by their strong and highly significant correlations with both human expert judgments and LLM-based evaluations.**

Table R2-1: the consistency among the scores from humans, the judger LLM, and our logicality metrics

|                      | Pearson | p        | Spearman | p        |
| -------------------- | ------- | -------- | -------- | -------- |
| Our Metrics vs Human | 0.7453  | 3.24e-10 | 0.7798   | 4.88e-10 |
| Our Metrics vs LLM   | 0.7860  | 2.07e-10 | 0.8303   | 2.89e-10 |
| Human vs LLM         | 0.8078  | 1.27e-10 | 0.8299   | 2.43e-10 |

## Response to Question #2

> In Fig.3 Direct Sampling Baseline, did you make sure that $A^\prime$ is aligned with $A$ (or $\mathcal{N}$)? Since  is curated answer, it is more likely to be of higher quality and correct. Could this be the reason that logic-guided sampling achieved better performance?

Thank you for your question. Following the practice adopted in many existing distillation-based studies [1,2], we use a rejection sampling strategy during distillation to ensure that the answer $A'$ produced by the distilled model is consistent with the original ground-truth answer $A$. Specifically, for multiple-choice and numeric-calculation problems (which account for more than three quarters of all questions), we perform rule-based verification to check correctness; for proof-style questions and expression-derivation problems, we rely on an LLM-as-a-judge approach to determine whether the final answer is correct. If the distilled model produces an incorrect answer, we prompt it to regenerate; samples that remain incorrect after a maximum number of attempts are discarded. In this way, **we guarantee that all training samples have correct final answers, so that the only difference between "Logic-Distill" and "Direct-Distill" lies in the logicality of the reasoning process.**

We apologize for the confusion caused by not explaining this mechanism in detail in the original paper due to space limitations. **We have clarified these details in the revised paper and illustrate them intuitively in Figure 3.**

[1] Zelikman, E., Wu, Y., Mu, J., & Goodman, N. D. (2024). Star: Self-taught reasoner bootstrapping reasoning with reasoning. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems.

[2] Tong, Y., Zhang, X., Wang, R., Wu, R., & He, J. (2024). Dart-math: Difficulty-aware rejection tuning for mathematical problem-solving. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems.

## Response to Question #3

> Following Question 2, if all three data sampling methods have the same set of questions $Q$ and final answer $A$, would the improvements of logic-guided sampling still be as much?

As described in "Response to Question #2" above, we have ensured during data construction that every sample in the entire dataset contains a correct final answer. **This guarantees that the difference between the compared methods lies solely in the logicality of the reasoning process.** Therefore, our experimental conclusions are fully fair and valid.

summary.value:
The paper explores how to improve the scientific logicality of large language models in physics reasoning. The authors argue that current reasoning models often produce fragmented and loosely connected reasoning chains that lack human-like logical coherence. To address this issue, they propose a Scientific Logicality Enriched Methodology with three quantitative measures, which are logical fidelity, causal connection, and inferential progress, to evaluate and enhance reasoning quality. They also build a physics-specific dataset where each problem is annotated with logical nexuses that capture the essential steps of scientific reasoning.

Based on this framework, the authors propose two logic-guided data sampling methods for supervised fine-tuning: Reasoning Style Transfer (RST), which turns structured logical nexuses into natural-language reasoning, and Logical-Distillation (L-D), which selects high-logicality samples for training. Experiments on their PHYSLOGIC benchmark and several public physics QA datasets show that these methods improve both reasoning coherence and answer accuracy, suggesting that incorporating logical structure into training data can strengthen scientific reasoning ability.

strengths.value: The paper tackles an underexplored but meaningful problem of improving the logical coherence of scientific reasoning in LLMs. Its proposed framework divides reasoning quality into measurable components such as logical fidelity, causal connection, and inferential progress, providing a structured basis for studying logic-aware model training in the future.

weaknesses.value:
1. The definition of the ground truth logical nexus is potentially unstable. Scientific reasoning problems often admit multiple valid solution paths, and some reasoning steps can be rearranged or occur in parallel without affecting correctness. The authors do not discuss how such variability is handled. If many correct nexuses are omitted or only one canonical sequence is annotated, the proposed metrics may underestimate model performance and weaken the validity of the conclusions.

2. In Table 4, the out-of-domain results show very limited improvement on the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B model, suggesting that the claimed generalization benefit may not hold consistently across architectures.

3. The data scales used for RST (80k) and Logic-Distill (40k) differ substantially, which makes it difficult to attribute performance differences purely to the proposed methodology. Although Section 4.4 includes a scaling-law analysis, the discussion remains qualitative and does not include experiments where both methods are trained on exactly the same number of samples, making it unclear how much of the reported gain comes from logicality rather than data quantity.

4. The evaluation heavily relies on the authors’ own logicality metrics (logical fidelity, causal connection, and inferential progress), which are derived from the same annotated nexus structure used for training. This creates a strong overlap between the training signal and the evaluation criteria. Without human judgments or external benchmarks, it is difficult to confirm whether higher metric scores truly correspond to more logically sound reasoning, or simply reflect closer alignment to the annotated schema. Moreover, the relationship between these logicality metrics and task accuracy has not been empirically demonstrated, leaving it unclear whether improvements in logicality genuinely translate into better reasoning performance.

## Response to Question #4

> How to get the Nexus and Weight for each question? Is the Nexus unique for a certain question? (Maybe we can combine the two steps in Nexus into a "bigger" one)

We thank the reviewer for this question. For each problem, the logical nexuses and their importance weights are automatically extracted by a strong LLM from the derivation part of the source paper. Specifically, each formula in the derivation is associated with one logical nexus, and its importance weight is determined based on the surrounding textual explanation before and after the formula. The full prompts used for this extraction procedure are provided in Section G.3.

In addition, we conducted a human quality check: two physics experts evaluated both the quality of the extracted nexuses and their consistency with the original papers. As shown in Table 11 in Section D.2, the human scores for Nexus Quality are above 90 points, **which strongly supports the correctness of the automatically extracted nexuses and their corresponding weights.**

## Response to Question #5

> In your metrics, you mainly use the cosine similarity of text embeddings. Have you ever tried NLI models.

Thanks for this suggestion. In the reasoning-step segmentation stage, we first decompose a complete reasoning trajectory into a sequence of semantically relatively independent sentences, and at this stage we only need to measure how well each sentence aligns semantically with the corresponding logical nexus in text space; we do not explicitly model causal or contradiction relations between sentences here. Given this design objective, and considering the requirements of runtime efficiency, scalability, and ease of reproducibility in large-scale scientific reasoning settings, we adopt cosine similarity over pre-trained sentence embeddings as the underlying mechanism for text semantic matching. Higher-level logical properties such as the consistency of the reasoning chain, its causal ordering, and its non-redundant forward progress are then captured in the subsequent construction of the $\mathcal{F}$/$\mathcal{O}$/$\mathcal{P}$ metrics through the global distribution and matching structure of these similarities, without requiring a standalone NLI classifier to assign pair-wise labels. We agree that NLI-style models are a promising direction and may provide complementary signals, and we plan to explore them in our future work.

## Response to Question #6

> I am also curious whether Logical Nexus is specific to physics reasoning? It seems that we could also define "Nexus" or extract it using your prompt for other domains (math, other STEM domains).

Logical nexuses are not specific to physics reasoning; the core idea applies equally well to other domains such as mathematics, chemistry, and biology. Our method is therefore not intrinsically restricted to physics, and the prompting/extraction pipeline can in principle be adapted to other STEM fields. We choose physics as an exemplar discipline because its reasoning paradigm naturally spans formal derivation and computation in formal sciences (e.g., pure math), as well as real-world modeling and experimental methodology in natural science (e.g., biology and chemistry). We appreciate your suggestion very much and plan to extend our study of scientific logicality to additional disciplines in future work.

## Response to Weakness #4

> The proposed metrics heavily rely on "reasoning step segmentation." How to segment such long responses from large reasoning models into "reasoning steps"? I think there is no consensus on this problem, and I believe a different segmentation strategy will influence these metrics.

The reasoning-step segmentation in our work is implemented by a rule-based procedure that splits a long model response into a sequence of semantically relatively independent sentences, using punctuation such as periods, question marks, and line breaks as boundaries. We agree with the reviewer that different segmentation strategies can influence the metrics. In our early experiments, we found that: 

- Using overly fine-grained clause-level segmentation leads to segments that are too short to express a complete semantic unit; 
- Segmenting by ordered lists or section headers is unreliable because not all LLMs answer in list or multi-level heading formats; 
- And using an LLM or an end-to-end learned segmentation model would introduce substantial computational overhead.

Taken together, sentence-level rule-based segmentation offers a good balance between semantic completeness, robustness to heterogeneous output formats, and evaluation efficiency.

Consistent with our observations, sentence-level rule-based segmentation is also the most common design in recent process-evaluation studies of chain-of-thought reasoning [1-3]. **We have added a detailed description of our segmentation procedure in the revised paper (line 105), which is highlighted in red.** We also sincerely appreciate your valuable suggestion. We agree that a robust semantic segmentation method is essential for ensuring reliable and trustworthy evaluation metrics. In future work, we plan to further investigate this problem in greater depth.

[1] Macar, U., Bogdan, P. C., Rajamanoharan, S., & Nanda, N. Chain-of-Thought Resampling for Interpreting LLM Decision-Making. In Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at NeurIPS 2025.

[2] Sun, H., Sakai, Y., Sakajo, H., Ozaki, S., Hayashi, K., Kamigaito, H., & Watanabe, T. (2025, November). LoCt-Instruct: An Automatic Pipeline for Constructing Datasets of Logical Continuous Instructions. In Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing.

[3] Lightman, H., Kosaraju, V., Burda, Y., Edwards, H., Baker, B., Lee, T., ... & Cobbe, K. (2023, May). Let's verify step by step. In The Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations.

## Response to Weakness #2

> As the PHYSLOGIC is collected from arXiv papers. It is possible that PHYSLOGIC has a data contamination issue.

We sincerely thank you for this valuable suggestion. In this work, we take special care to avoid data contamination:

- First, the PHYSLOGIC dataset is constructed from recently published, research-level physics papers (from 2025 onward). The problems and derivations in these papers are more specialized and novel, which greatly reduces the likelihood of overlap with widely used training corpora based on textbooks and exam materials.
- Second, in our experiments, both the backbone LLMs used for training and the public benchmarks used for evaluation are deliberately chosen to be released before 2025, so that the experimental results are not affected by data contamination.
- Third, although it is impossible to completely eliminate temporal mismatch when evaluating the latest closed-source models (such as GPT-5), we observe no substantial performance gap between these models and pre-2025 models on our benchmark, which further suggests that data contamination in our dataset is limited.
- Finally, our data construction pipeline is described in a modular and transparent manner and is highly portable. This makes it straightforward to periodically instantiate new variants such as "PHYSLOGIC-2026" from future physics papers, allowing the benchmark to be updated over time and remain robust to potential data leakage.

## Response to Weakness #1

> The definition of the ground truth logical nexus is potentially unstable. Scientific reasoning problems often admit multiple valid solution paths, and some reasoning steps can be rearranged or occur in parallel without affecting correctness. The authors do not discuss how such variability is handled. If many correct nexuses are omitted or only one canonical sequence is annotated, the proposed metrics may underestimate model performance and weaken the validity of the conclusions.

Thank you for raising this concern. We agree that, from the perspective of objective dependency, certain reasoning steps can be permuted or executed in parallel. However, when humans solve a scientific problem, these steps are always organized in some sequential manner. This ordered reasoning pattern is exactly the natural scientific logic that we hope LLMs can learn. Accordingly, in this work we construct our dataset from academic papers. For a given scientific problem, we assume that the solution strategy adopted by the paper’s author reflects higher logicality among multiple possible derivation paths; thus, we use it to define the logical nexuses. Moreover, as the dataset grows, papers on the same research topic naturally introduce diversity and variability in scientific reasoning, while still preserving overall scientific logicality.

In addition, as shown in Figure 1, our defined logical nexuses summarize higher-level reasoning behaviors, each of which contains several concrete sub-steps. Consequently, permutations in the order of these sub-steps do not affect the final evaluation results.

## Response to Weakness #2

> In Table 4, the out-of-domain results show very limited improvement on the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B model, suggesting that the claimed generalization benefit may not hold consistently across architectures.

Thanks for pointing out this. In our experiments we observe that, when we **continue SFT on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (hereafter "R1-7B")**, the model's performance on public benchmarks exhibits a "first drop, then recovery" pattern. This is because R1-7B itself is already a backbone model with strong reasoning ability and its own reasoning style, and the change in reasoning style/output format induced by the training data leads to a distribution shift, which can weaken the effectiveness of SFT and may even harm its existing instruction-following ability. Several existing SFT studies have also confirmed this observation [1,2]. 

**For GPQA and SciBench benchmarks**, which only require returning a single answer judged by rules, such changes in style can amplify errors at the extraction and formatting level [3]. For example, the answer option appearing multiple times before and after the final answer, or extra verbal expressions surrounding a numeric value, even if the model's underlying physics reasoning ability is not degraded. In contrast, the evaluation pipeline of PhysReason checks the whole process and relies on LLM-as-a-judge scoring, and is therefore more tolerant to expression form and process style, allowing it to benefit more directly from improvements in derivation ability.

Finally, and most importantly, as discussed above, all SFT settings lead to some performance drop of R1-7B on the first two benchmarks (Table 7). However, compared with other baselines, our "Logic-Distill" and "RST" settings yield the smallest drops on GPQA-D(Phy.) and SciBench(Phy.), while at the same time achieving **more balanced results across all three benchmarks**, with overall **average improvements of +1.92 and +0.76** over the backbone model. The comparison with baselines under the same SFT settings demonstrates the effectiveness, robustness, and generalization of our constructed datasets across different backbone models.

[1] Yang, L., Huang, J. T., Lu, Y., Li, Z. J., & Xue, G. (2025, November). The Emperor's New Reasoning: Format Imitation Overshadows Genuine Mathematical Understanding in SFT. In Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing.

[2] Yu, B., Yuan, H., Li, H., Xu, X., Wei, Y., Wang, B., ... & Chen, K. (2025). Long-short chain-of-thought mixture supervised fine-tuning eliciting efficient reasoning in large language models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.03469.

[3] Molfese, F. M., Moroni, L., Gioffré, L., Scirè, A., Conia, S., & Navigli, R. (2025). Right Answer, Wrong Score: Uncovering the Inconsistencies of LLM Evaluation in Multiple-Choice Question Answering. In Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics.

Dear Area Chair,

We sincerely thank you and the reviewers for the time and effort devoted to assessing our submission. Below we briefly summarize the discussion phase and the corresponding revisions.

First, we appreciate that all four reviewers acknowledge the contribution and novelty of this work. They note that we address **an underexplored but important problem** of faithfully measuring and improving the logicality of physics/scientific reasoning in LLMs using explicitly quantifiable dimensions *(mG7H, dY1b, Sq3b)*. Reviewers also highlight our multi-faceted logicality formulation and logic-guided sampling strategy, **which support a high-quality SFT corpus** and the PHYSLOGIC benchmark with reasoning gains beyond data scaling *(mG7H, JveH, Sq3b)*. Finally, they find the **experiments comprehensive** and the **presentation sufficiently detailed** *(JveH, Sq3b)*.

Second, in response to the weaknesses and questions raised during review and discussion, we have made the following clarifications and additions in the revised version:

1. On the empirical validation of the three logicality metrics *(dY1b, Sq3b)* and the need for more case studies *(JveH)*: **we added three empirical studies** showing that the metrics reflect logicality in practice, and **included case studies**. These have been incorporated into Section 4.2 and Appendix J of the revised paper.

2. On the behavior of the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B model after continued-SFT *(mG7H, dY1b)*: **we provided a more detailed analysis** of the causes from both the continued-SFT and evaluation perspectives, and showed that under the same SFT settings our configurations achieve **better and more balanced performance** than other baselines.

3. On the lack of some experiments, such as cross-domain OOD evaluation *(JveH, Sq3b)*, ablations over different logicality percentiles *(Sq3b)*, and reporting logicality scores on the training sets *(Sq3b)*: following the their suggestions, **we added the corresponding experiments and analyses**. These results are presented in Appendix D of the revised paper.

4. On lower-level design choices in our pipeline, including reasoning-step segmentation *(mG7H, Sq3b)*, sentence-encoder similarity *(mG7H, JveH)*, and greedy matching *(dY1b)*: we have provided **more detailed motivation** and **implementation descriptions**, and support these design choices with additional experiments and related-work discussion.

5. On various details of the logicality evaluation and data-sampling procedures, such as the amount of data used for distillation *(dY1b, Sq3b)*, reasoning-style transfer *(mG7H, dY1b)*, the specification of the logicality metrics *(JveH, Sq3b)*, and the correctness of answers in the training data *(JveH)*: **we have addressed these points one by one** in the rebuttal and clarified them in the revised paper to improve the overall presentation.

In addition, during the discussion phase, reviewer JveH indicated that our response had **well addressed the concerns** and expressed willingness to **raise the score to 8**, while the other reviewers did not provide further comments.

Thank you for your time and we hope this summary is helpful for your decision.

Sincerely, Authors

The authors propose three new metrics to assess the logicality of an LLM’s reasoning process: Logical Fidelity, Causal Connection, and Inferential Progress.

summary.value:
This paper proposes a logicality-aware framework for evaluating and improving scientific reasoning in LLMs, including a logical-nexus annotation scheme, new metrics, and logic-guided data construction. While the topic is interesting, several core issues limit confidence in the conclusions.

First, the definition of ground-truth logical nexuses is potentially unstable. Scientific problems often admit multiple valid reasoning paths, yet the framework largely assumes a single canonical structure. It remains unclear how alternative but correct derivations are handled, raising concerns that the metrics may penalize valid reasoning and weaken evaluation reliability.

Second, the claimed generalization is not consistently supported. Out-of-domain results show only limited improvement on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, suggesting that the benefits may be model-dependent rather than robust across architectures.

Third, the evaluation relies heavily on the authors’ own logicality metrics, which are derived from the same annotations used for training and data selection. This tight coupling makes it difficult to verify that higher scores reflect genuinely better reasoning rather than closer alignment to the annotated schema, and the connection between logicality improvements and task accuracy is not convincingly established.

Finally, the framework depends critically on reasoning-step segmentation and embedding-based similarity. Different segmentation strategies could substantially affect the metrics, and compressing reasoning steps into sentence embeddings may lose fine-grained logical information, especially for complex problems.

In addition, the writing lacks clarity in several places, and the motivation for the specific design of the proposed logicality metrics is not clearly articulated, making it harder to assess their necessity and validity.

Overall, these concerns outweigh the reported gains, and I recommend rejection.

reviewer_concerns.value:
The rebuttal addresses several technical and presentation issues, including clearer descriptions of step segmentation, embedding-based matching, and additional ablations and analyses. These additions improve clarity but are largely incremental.

The core concerns remain. The definition of a single ground-truth logical nexus does not adequately account for multiple valid reasoning paths. Generalization remains inconsistent, with limited out-of-domain gains on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. Finally, the evaluation is still tightly coupled to the training annotations, leaving it unclear whether improved metric scores reflect genuine reasoning gains or alignment to the predefined schema.

Overall, the rebuttal does not sufficiently resolve the main conceptual and methodological issues.

reviewer_scores.value: Overall, while a reviewer would respond positively to the rebuttal, the remaining unresolved concerns suggest that reviewer consensus would still be mixed rather than clearly supportive, i.e., 4,4,8,6.

## Response to Question #2

> I understand that SFT typically operates on natural language sequences, but I am curious about the RST design choice. Since the logical nexuses already represent explicit reasoning structures, is converting them back into a natural-language reasoning chain essential? Would direct supervision over structured logic be more effective?

Thanks. Current backbone models such as Qwen2.5 and DeepSeek-R1 already exhibit a natural tendency to produce coherent natural-language chain-of-thought explanations as their default reasoning style. Prior work on reasoning distillation has shown that the reasoning style / output format of the supervision signal matters greatly [1], and that large changes in format (e.g., from fluent CoT to highly structured skeletons) can introduce distribution shift that weakens the effectiveness of SFT and may even harm existing instruction compliance ability.

For this reason, our RST design keeps supervision in the natural-language space: given the logical nexuses as a scaffold, the expert model generates a coherent reasoning chain that both respects the backbone’s native CoT style and aligns with the target logical structure. In our framework, logical nexuses primarily serve as high-level logical constraints and evaluation signals, rather than as a structured target for token-level supervision.

In fact, during the early stages of this work, we also tried a setting where the SFT data was obtained by directly concatenating the logical nexuses into a reasoning sequence. The results based on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B are summarized in the table below: this "direct nexus reasoning" variant performs clearly worse than the "RST" method, which supports the above design choice. 

| Training set  | GPQA-D    | SciBench  | PhysReason |
| ------------- | --------- | --------- | ---------- |
| logic-nexuses | 44.96     | 35.58     | 37.22      |
| RST           | **47.67** | **38.86** | **37.71**  |

[1] Yang, L., Huang, J. T., Lu, Y., Li, Z. J., & Xue, G. (2025, November). The Emperor’s New Reasoning: Format Imitation Overshadows Genuine Mathematical Understanding in SFT. In Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing.

## Response to Question #3

> Could the authors clarify why the RST and Logic-Distill datasets were constructed with different sample sizes? Was the smaller size of Logic-Distill due to high-score filtering, and have the authors examined whether the improvements stem from logicality rather than data quantity?

As explained above in our **"Response to Weakness #3"**, in our pipeline Logic-Distill is obtained by applying our logicality metrics to filter the full 80k candidate set (i.e., the "Direct-Distill" dataset), so its final size is indeed smaller than 80k. Appendix B (Tables 9–11) quantitatively shows that, at the same 20k and 40k training scales, Logic-Distill consistently achieves higher scores than the baselines on both the public physics benchmarks and the PhysLogic metric. Furthermore, **with only 40k training examples, Logic-Distill already outperforms the baselines trained on 80k examples.** This indicates that improving the logicality of the training data is more effective than merely increasing data volume: **using fewer but more logically consistent samples yields better performance than simply doubling the dataset without considering logicality.**

Dear Reviewer JveH,

We are truly grateful for your thoughtful and constructive comments on our submission.

In response to your review, we have:

1. clarified that we use a sentence encoder only as a low-level semantic representation for single-step units, and that our three metrics $\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{P}$ are defined as higher-level logical measures built on these similarities;

2. added a case-study section and a human-metric consistency study on 200 instances, showing strong and highly significant correlations between our logicality scores and both expert and LLM judgments;

3. clarified that objective accuracy in PhysLogic is computed only for multiple-choice and numeric problems, while proof-style items are used to evaluate scientific logicality via $\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{O}/\mathcal{P}$, and discussed future directions for rigorous proof evaluation;

4. added out-of-domain experiments on AIME25 and AMC, which show that physics-based logical training also improves math performance and that logic-guided settings outperform baselines; and

5. detailed our rejection-sampling pipeline ensuring that all compared datasets share the same questions and correct final answers, so that observed improvements arise from differences in reasoning logicality rather than label quality.

We have revised the paper accordingly, added the above supplementary experiments, and improved the overall presentation. Your suggestions are of great significance for improving our work. We would be very grateful and look forward to receiving your feedback on our responses during the discussion.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,
Authors

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the continued engagement. Below we respond to the additional questions.

## 1. Response regarding the math benchmarks

Thank you for raising this point. We have further refined our experimental setup and now evaluate on AIME2025 and AMC with 16 independent runs. The averaged results are shown in the table below:

|                      | AIME2025 | AMC       | Avg       |
| -------------------- | -------- | --------- | --------- |
| Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct | 6.04     | 39.61     | 22.83     |
| Direct-Distill       | 6.25     | 41.19     | 23.72     |
| Logic-Distill        | **8.54** | **43.15** | **25.85** |
| RST                  | 8.13     | 40.81     | 24.47     |

These results have been incorporated into the revised paper.

We also analyzed why RST is slightly worse than Logic-Distill on the math datasets. In Logic-Distill, the reasoning traces are generated by the teacher LLM (DeepSeek-R1), which contains rich numerical calculations and verification steps; the arithmetic involved in these physics problems appears to transfer well to the student model's mathematical abilities. By contrast, in RST, the reasoning traces are derived from the logical nexuses, with a higher proportion devoted to high-level logical structure and comparatively less emphasis on explicit numerical computation. As a result, RST is less effective than Logic-Distill at improving pure mathematical calculation skills.

## 2. Response regarding the sampling ratios in Logic-Distill

Thank you for this suggestion. Logic-Distill is in fact a subset selected from the "Direct-Distill" data, so different percentile thresholds naturally lead to different data scales. Therefore, in the additional experiments (Tables R3-1 and R3-2), to factor out the influence of data size, we evaluate all four percentile settings at a unified training size of 20k, i.e., on the checkpoints at 20k training examples. The superiority of the "top 25%" setting under this controlled setting provides strong evidence for the practical significance of our logicality-based selection.

In terms of absolute performance, the total amount of training data is also an important factor. As shown in Tables R3-1-a and R3-2-a below, the 40k "top 50%" configuration overall outperforms the 20k "top 25%" configuration. Admittedly, under a **fixed training scale, a more stringent filtering ratio tends to yield better performance**. However, due to resource and cost constraints, we were not able to construct a larger-scale dataset for the 25% setting. We therefore adopt the 50% threshold in the main experiments as a practical trade-off that **balances higher logicality with a larger data scale**. We have added a dedicated discussion of this design choice in the revised paper (line 1079).

**Table R3-1-a.** Ablation study (In-domain) under different percentile settings in "Logic-Distill" (evaluated on the final checkpoint).

| Data Sampled Rate of L-D | Data Scale | F         | O         | P        | Acc       |
| ------------------------ | ---------- | --------- | --------- | -------- | --------- |
| 25%                      | 20k        | 50.01     | 69.34     | 4.78     | **41.59** |
| 50%                      | 40k        | **53.98** | **69.39** | **4.97** | 40.97     |

**Table R3-2-a.** Ablation study (Out-of-domain) under different percentile settings in "Logic-Distill" (evaluated on the final checkpoint).

| Data Sampled Rate of L-D | Data Scale | GPQA-D    | SciBench  | PhysReason |
| ------------------------ | ---------- | --------- | --------- | ---------- |
| 25%                      | 20k        | 32.56     | 35.92     | 40.30      |
| 50%                      | 40k        | **43.02** | **49.22** | **42.88**  |

## 3. Response regarding process segmentation

Thank you for voicing this concern. We would like to clarify that, similar to our approach, *Let's verify step by step*[1] also uses a rule-based method to segment reasoning steps (based on line breaks). To improve the robustness of this rule-based segmentation, they explicitly train the answering LLM to follow a line-by-line reasoning format; the training data are generated by a few-shot generator (see Section 2.3 of that paper), and human annotators only label the correctness of the reasoning steps (see Section 2.4 of that paper).

In our setting, to ensure the fairness of the evaluation, we do not further fine-tune the evaluated LLMs for reasoning format. We fully share and appreciate your emphasis on the importance of process segmentation. As a direction for future work, we plan to explore more effective and accurate segmentation methods, such as training a dedicated segmentation model, standardizing the output formats of the evaluated models, or leveraging LLM-based segmentation.

[1] Lightman, H., Kosaraju, V., Burda, Y., Edwards, H., Baker, B., Lee, T., ... & Cobbe, K. (2023, May). Let's verify step by step. In The Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations.

## Response to Weakness #2

> The effectiveness seems to be undermined with reasoning-based model (the Qwen-distill ones) where the original model achieves the best performance on two of the benchmarks.

Thanks for pointing out this. In our experiments we observe that, when we **continue SFT on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (hereafter "R1-7B")**, the model's performance on public benchmarks exhibits a "first drop, then recovery" pattern. This is because R1-7B itself is already a backbone model with strong reasoning ability and its own reasoning style, and the change in reasoning style/output format induced by the training data leads to a distribution shift, which can weaken the effectiveness of SFT and may even harm its existing instruction-following ability. Several existing SFT studies have also confirmed this observation [1,2]. 

**For GPQA and SciBench benchmarks**, which only require returning a single answer judged by rules, such changes in style can amplify errors at the extraction and formatting level [3]. For example, the answer option appearing multiple times before and after the final answer, or extra verbal expressions surrounding a numeric value, even if the model's underlying physics reasoning ability is not degraded. In contrast, the evaluation pipeline of PhysReason checks the whole process and relies on LLM-as-a-judge scoring, and is therefore more tolerant to expression form and process style, allowing it to benefit more directly from improvements in derivation ability.

Finally, and most importantly, as discussed above, all SFT settings lead to some performance drop of R1-7B on the first two benchmarks (Table 7). However, compared with other baselines, our "Logic-Distill" and "RST" settings yield the smallest drops on GPQA-D(Phy.) and SciBench(Phy.), while at the same time achieving **more balanced results across all three benchmarks**, with overall **average improvements of +1.92 and +0.76** over the backbone model. The comparison with baselines under the same SFT settings demonstrates the effectiveness, robustness, and generalization of our constructed datasets across different backbone models.

[1] Yang, L., Huang, J. T., Lu, Y., Li, Z. J., & Xue, G. (2025, November). The Emperor's New Reasoning: Format Imitation Overshadows Genuine Mathematical Understanding in SFT. In Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing.

[2] Yu, B., Yuan, H., Li, H., Xu, X., Wei, Y., Wang, B., ... & Chen, K. (2025). Long-short chain-of-thought mixture supervised fine-tuning eliciting efficient reasoning in large language models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.03469.

[3] Molfese, F. M., Moroni, L., Gioffré, L., Scirè, A., Conia, S., & Navigli, R. (2025). Right Answer, Wrong Score: Uncovering the Inconsistencies of LLM Evaluation in Multiple-Choice Question Answering. In Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics.

Dear Reviewer dY1b,

We are truly grateful for your thoughtful and constructive comments on our submission.

In response to your review, we have:

1. clarified how ground-truth logical nexuses are defined from academic papers as higher-level reasoning units, and why permutations of lower-level sub-steps or multiple valid solution paths do not undermine evaluation stability;

2. analyzed why continuing SFT on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B can inherently underperform on some benchmarks, and shown that under the same SFT settings our Logic-Distill and RST configurations achieve better and more balanced performance than other baselines;

3. clarified in the paper that our existing same-scale ablation studies (20k/40k/60k) already disentangle logicality-based gains from mere data volume quantitatively;

4. added three empirical studies demonstrating human/LLM–metric consistency, before/after training improvements in reasoning logicality, and a strong correlation between logicality scores and final task accuracy; and

5. included a dynamic-programming alignment ablation for logical fidelity and a comparison between RST and a direct-nexus reasoning variant.

Your suggestions are of great significance for improving our work. We would be very grateful and look forward to receiving your feedback on our responses during the discussion.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,
Authors

## Response to Question #1

> How do you judge the answer correctness of those open-ended questions on PHYSLOGIC? Are you relying on the rule-based method?

Thank you for raising this question. In our PHYSLOGIC benchmark, we evaluate two complementary aspects of model performance: the logicality of the reasoning process and the correctness of the final answer. For the latter, the physics domain currently lacks a rigorous and objective methodology for verifying the correctness of proofs or open-ended derivations. **To ensure that final-answer accuracy remains strictly objective, reproducible, and minimally affected by ambiguous scoring criteria**, we compute accuracy only on multiple-choice and numeric-calculation problems.

**Nevertheless, the proof-style and open-ended derivation problems in our benchmark remain essential.** The three logicality dimensions we design  provide a principled way to characterize the scientific logicality of LLMs when they solve proof or open-ended physics problems, and they allow us to examine whether our proposed training methods also improve reasoning quality on such open-form questions.

Finally, **as an important direction for future work, we will further explore how to reliably evaluate the correctness of open-ended physics reasoning.** One possible approach is to use adversarial question-answering procedures to test the logical robustness and causal vulnerability of the derivation chain.

## Response to Question #2

> I am curious about the range of the proposed three metrics.

Thanks for your question. All three metrics ($\mathcal{F}$, $\mathcal{O}$, and $\mathcal{P}$) take values in the range $[0, 1]$, where 1 corresponds to perfect alignment with the logical nexuses. In our experiments, all reported values are presented in percentage form. We have explained in detail the definition and value range of the above indicators in the revised paper.

## Response to Question #3

> How to set the coefficients in the formula in L225?

Thanks. Section F.1 reports the values of the three coefficients and presents a detailed sensitivity analysis of the model performance under different weight settings.

## Response to Weakness #1

> Although there are various ways to create such high-quality dataset for training, the entire pipeline relies on the dot-product of step representations, which is conducted through a sentence encoder and would bear significant information compression loss. Therefore the reliability of metrics derives from the embedding dot products becomes questionable specially for problems of higher complexities.

Thank you for raising this concern. In our method, sentence embeddings are used only to represent the semantic similarity between each sentence in the model-generated reasoning trace and each ground-truth logical nexus, via the dot product between their embeddings. This is a well-established and widely adopted practice in NLP research and engineering applications [1-3]. We do not directly treat these similarity values as the final metric scores. Instead, as described in Section 2.1, we use the relative distribution of similarities across all sentence-nexus pairs to evaluate how well the model's reasoning logic aligns with the ground-truth logical structure. 

For problems with higher complexity, although the raw reasoning traces become longer, we first decompose them into a sequence of semantically independent sentences (see "Response to Question #2" for details). Table R1-1 reports the average logical-nexus length in our benchmark dataset and the average sentence length in LLM-generated reasoning trajectories (using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as an example). Prior work indicates that encoding such short, focused segments as sentence embeddings helps keep semantic information loss due to fixed-dimensional compression at a relatively low level [4,5].

Table R1-1 Sentence Length Statistics

|                | Logical nexus | LLM's reasoning sentence |
| -------------- | ------------- | ------------------------ |
| Average length | 21.84         | 27.62                    |

[1] Das, S., Deb, N., Cortesi, A., & Chaki, N. (2021). Sentence embedding models for similarity detection of software requirements. SN Computer Science.

[2] Reimers, N., & Gurevych, I. (2019, November). Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks. In Proceedings of the 2019 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing and the 9th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing.

[3] https://sbert.net/examples/sentence_transformer/training/sts/README.html

[4] Adi, Y., Kermany, E., Belinkov, Y., Lavi, O., & Goldberg, Y. (2017, January). Fine-grained analysis of sentence embeddings using auxiliary prediction tasks. In 5th International Conference on Learning Representations.

[5] Sannigrahi, S., van Genabith, J., & España-Bonet, C. (2023, May). Are the Best Multilingual Document Embeddings simply Based on Sentence Embeddings?. In Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics.

## Response to Weakness #3

> While PhysLogic covered proof questions, the authors did not establish a robust way of evaluating LLM generated proofs, making these type of data less meaningful.

Thank you for raising this question. In our PhysLogic benchmark, we evaluate two complementary aspects of model performance: the logicality of the reasoning process and the correctness of the final answer. For the latter, the physics domain currently lacks a rigorous and objective methodology for verifying the correctness of proofs or open-ended derivations. **To ensure that final-answer accuracy remains strictly objective, reproducible, and minimally affected by ambiguous scoring criteria**, we compute accuracy only on multiple-choice and numeric-calculation problems.

**Nevertheless, the proof-style and open-ended derivation problems in our benchmark remain essential.** The three logicality dimensions we design, which show high consistency with human expert judgments in our human study (see Response to Weakness #2 above), provide a principled way to characterize the scientific logicality of LLMs when they solve proof or open-ended physics problems, and they allow us to examine whether our proposed training methods also improve reasoning quality on such open-form questions.

Finally, **as an important direction for future work, we will further explore how to reliably evaluate the correctness of open-ended physics reasoning.** One possible approach is to use adversarial question–answering procedures to test the logical robustness and causal vulnerability of the derivation chain.

## Response to Question #1

> When finetuned for logical reasoning on physics questions, how does that affect out-of-domain performances, such as on math benchmarks?

We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. we have added an experiment where, using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the backbone, we compare the base model, "Direct-Distill", "Logic-Distill", and "RST" variants on two math benchmarks: "AIME25" and "AMC" (average of 8 repetitions). The results are reported in Table RQ1-1 below. Experimental results show that although our constructed dataset is purely physical, it still delivers improvements on the mathematical benchmark, and the logic-guided settings also outperform the baseline, demonstrating the interdisciplinary generalization of our proposed method.

RQ1-1 OOD experiment results on math benchmarks

| setting             | AIME25 | AMC   | Average   |
| ------------------- | -------- | ----- | ----- |
| Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct | 5.83     | 38.86 | 22.35 |
| Direct-Distill      | 6.25     | 42.17 | 24.21 |
| Logic-Distill       | **8.75**   | **44.88** | **26.82** |
| RST                 | 7.92     | 39.46 | 23.69 |

The above experimental results have been updated in our revised paper (Appendix D.1), which are highlighted in red.

## Response to Question #1

> I am still not clear about how the reasoning style transfer is conducted in terms of the incorporation of the weighted nexuses. Are they directly fed into the model generator?

Thank you for the question. As shown in Appendix H.2, in the Reasoning Style Transfer stage, we serialize the logical nexuses and their importance weights into a textual list of key solution points; see also Appendix H.3), and include this list in the prompt together with (1) the original exam question and (2) a human problem-solving thought-process example. A strong LLM is then instructed to transform this weighted nexus list into a coherent, first-person reasoning narrative that follows the intended logical order and preserves the scientific content.

## Response to Question #2

> What is the step separation strategy to segment the reasoning traces if not specified, I was not able to find it?

Thank you for pointing out this missing detail. For all generated reasoning traces, we perform rule-based sentence-level segmentation, which is the most common design in recent process-evaluation studies of chain-of-thought reasoning [1-3]. Specifically, we split the model's reasoning text at end-of-sentence punctuation (periods and question marks) and line breaks, and treat each resulting sentence as one reasoning step: $r_i$, forming $R=\{r1,\cdots,r_m\}$.

We adopt sentence-level segmentation because it avoids overly fragmented clauses and does not rely on any model-specific formatting conventions, offering a good balance between semantic completeness, robustness to heterogeneous output formats, and evaluation efficiency. **We have clarified this step separation strategy in the revised paper (line 105), which is highlighted in red.**

By contrast, the ground-truth logical nexuses are not obtained by splitting model reasoning, but are extracted directly from the reference papers using a strong-LLM prompt as shown in Appendix H.3.

## Response to Weakness #5

> I recommend that the authors spend more text explaining the definition of the new metrics, especially Causal Connection. It is not very intuitive to see the meaning from the formula.

We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. Below we provide an intuitive and detailed explanation of the three logicality metrics we propose:

1. **Logical Fidelity**: This dimension measures the unordered alignment between the LLM’s generated reasoning steps and the ground-truth logical nexuses. Conceptually, it is the harmonic mean of *Logic Precision* (the proportion of the model’s reasoning steps that are logically valid) and *Logic Recall* (the proportion of logical nexuses that are covered by the model’s reasoning).
2. **Causal Connection**: This dimension considers whether the LLM preserves the correct ordering between pairs of logical nexuses that have an inherent causal or derivational direction. When the model touches on both nexuses during reasoning, we examine whether the order it presents is consistent with the ground truth. This consistency is determined based on the relative distribution of semantic similarities.
3. **Inferential Progress**: This dimension captures whether the model’s reasoning progresses steadily toward the final answer. If the LLM repeatedly circles back to previously covered propositions or oscillates between them without making forward progress, the score on this dimension decreases.

In the revised paper, we have expanded and further clarify the explanations for all three metrics (highlighted in red).

## Response to Question #1

> In the computation of logical fidelity, the greedy matching strategy seems overly simplistic. Would more structured alignment methods (e.g., dynamic programming or global matching) yield more reliable results?

We appreciate your suggestion. In this work, we use a greedy matching strategy for computing logical fidelity mainly for computational efficiency, since the metric needs to be evaluated many times over long reasoning trajectories across datasets and models. More complex global alignment methods would substantially increase the runtime of our evaluation pipeline. 

In response to this question, we additionally implement a dynamic-programming–based global alignment method and recompute the logical fidelity scores for all evaluated models on the same set of reasoning processes. The results are summarized in Table RQ1-1 below. In addition, Table RQ1-2 reports the runtime efficiency of the two matching methods (average time per data instance). Empirically, dynamic-programming–based scores are highly consistent (relative deviation < 3%) with those from greedy matching: model rankings and performance trends remain stable under both strategies, while dynamic programming is substantially less efficient than the greedy matching algorithm. This indicates that our conclusions are not sensitive to the specific matching strategy and that the proposed greedy matching is a robust and efficient choice for computing logical fidelity. **We have added the above experimental results and discussion to the revised paper (Appendix D.2), and the newly added parts are highlighted in red.**
